rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause reassures the Messenger and urges him to steady himself and endure what is inevitable.
rows.anchor: تثبيت لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وبعث على أن يطامن نفسه الكريمة على احتماله

rows.speaker: التبيان في أقسام القرآن
rows.claim: A third reading says the Prophet is treated as lawful prey for killing and expulsion in the sanctuary whose people violate its protections.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية قول ثالث، وهو أن المعنى: وأنت مُستَحَلّ قتلُك وإخراجك من هذا البلد الأمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ḥill can mean lawful rather than sacred: on the conquest day the Prophet could lawfully kill whom he wished in Mecca.
rows.anchor: ومن معاني (الحِلّ) أنها تأتي بمعنى الحلال ضد الحرام

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf reads ḥill prospectively: at the conquest the Prophet may do as he wishes, including killing and capture, like the future sense in 39:30.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) : "يعني وأنت حِلّ به في المستقبل، تصنع فيه ما تريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under these last two interpretations, lā is negative: the oath is withheld because the people profane the sanctuary or the Prophet’s dignity there.
rows.anchor: فعلى كلا القولين: تكون (لا) نافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the sanctuary’s violations, the Messenger’s hardship, and his abuse makes a description of security ill-fitting here.
rows.anchor: أنه لما جرى ذِكْرُ المكابدة في هذا البلد، وما استحل به من الحرمات وما أصاب الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم من المشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the place secure would also clash with the interpretation that the Prophet may kill and capture there at the conquest.
rows.anchor: كما لا يصح ذكر ذلك على معنى أنه حِلٌّ لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يصنع فيه ما يشاء من القتل والأسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s atmosphere of hardship and its focus on disbelievers’ everlasting punishment likewise do not suit the epithet secure.
rows.anchor: كما أن جو السورة لا يناسب ذكر الأمن، فإن جو السورة في المكابدة والمشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating a word can be eloquent when Arabs want to draw attention, suspense, grief, exaltation, or awe; a poet’s repeated call illustrates this.
rows.anchor: أن العرب إذا عُنيت بلفظٍ كررته وذلك كأن يكون في موطن التشويق أو التحسر أو التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem’s repeated address يا موقد النار is an especially beautiful example of repetition for suspense and emphasis.
rows.anchor: قول الشاعر: يا مُوقد النار بالهنديِّ والغارِ ... هيّجت لي حَزَناً يا مُوقد النار

rows.speaker: أبو العتاهية
rows.claim: Abu al-Atahiya repeats Saʿid ibn Wahb’s name in a lament to intensify grief.
rows.anchor: ونحوه قول أبي العتاهية: مات والله سعيد بن وهب ... رحم الله سعيد بن وهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic repetition can magnify and instill awe, as in al-Haqqa, al-Qariʿa, and the companions of the right; it can also warn, as in al-Aʿraf.
rows.anchor: ومن التكرير للتعظيم والتهويل قوله تعالى: {الحاقة * وَمَآ أَدْرَاكَ مَا الحاقة}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition can also be reproachful denial, illustrated by a series of questions condemning someone who mistreats his benefactor.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون التكرير للإنكار وذلك كأن تقول لشخص أساء إلى مَنْ أحسن إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating this land exalts Mecca’s sanctity and highlights the injustice of the Messenger suffering there, where the fearful, wild animals, and birds are safe.
rows.anchor: والتكرار في الآية لتعظيم بلد الله الحرام فقد قال: {لاَ أُقْسِمُ بهاذا البلد * وَأَنتَ حِلٌّ بهاذا البلد}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites Malaak al-Tawil on the Arab habit of repeating expressions they care about, a feature of eloquent speech.
rows.anchor: أن العرب مهما اعتنت بشيء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says the land is normally sacred, but was made lawful for the Prophet at the conquest, so its two descriptions make it seem like two lands.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن التكرير جيء به لفائدة أخرى وهي أن هذا البلد حرام لا تُستحل حرمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites al-Durra on when repeated wording is apt: the second use has a distinct quality and ruling.
rows.anchor: إذا عني بالثاني غير المقصود بالأول من وصف يوجب له حكماً غير حكم الأول كان من مختار الكلام

rows.speaker: درة التنزيل
rows.claim: The first Mecca is the revered sanctuary, while the second is the same land made lawful for the Prophet in honor of his rank.
rows.anchor: فالبلد في الأول محرم وفي الثاني محلل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the father and offspring as Adam and his descendants, pairing the origin of the land, Mecca, with the origin of its people, Adam.
rows.anchor: فقيل: هو آدم وذريته "وعلى هذا فقد تضمن القسم، أصل المكان وأصل السكان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the father and offspring with the Messenger and his ancestors, linking the oath to his birthplace, his father’s sanctuary, and Ishmael.
rows.anchor: وقيل: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وآباؤه فعلى هذا "أقسم ببلده الذي هو مسقط رأسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the wording generally, covering every parent and offspring, including all animals.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ذلك. قال: هو على العموم يدخل فيه جميع الحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the universal reading, which includes all parents and children as well as the specific examples proposed by earlier interpreters.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي يترجح عندي فهو يشمل كل والد وولده يدخل فيه ما ذكره الأولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human assumes there will be no resurrection and that God cannot punish or requite him for what he has done.
rows.anchor: أنْ لن تقوم قيامة، ولن يقدر على الانتقام منه وعلى مكأفاته بما هو عليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says the threat is directed only at whoever deserves it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن التهديد "مصروف لمن يستحقه"

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies the referent as the human created in toil and asks whether he thinks nobody can overpower him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن المعنيَّ به الإنسان، أي: أيظن هذا الإنسان الذي خلق مكابداً شديداً

rows.speaker: البحر المحيط
rows.claim: Al-Bahr says the pronoun refers to the human, whose resolve, strength, and resources make him think no one can resist or overpower him.
rows.anchor: جاء في (البحر المحيط) : "والظاهر أن الضمير في {أَيَحْسَبُ} عائد على الإنسان

rows.speaker: التبيان
rows.claim: The creator who gave humans strength is even more able than they are; this independently proves divine power, knowledge, and the ability to requite deeds.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (التبيان) : "ثم أنكر سبحانه على الإنسان ظنه وحسبانه أن لن يقدر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the human was created to endure hardship, he must have been made strong enough to bear it; this connects the claim to the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: فالذي خُلق يكابد المصائب والمشاق لا بد أن يكون خُلق مستعدّاً لاحتمال ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad means much accumulated together, from the verb for something clumping together.
rows.anchor: اللبد: هو الكثير المجتمع من تَلَبَّدَ الشيءُ إذا اجتمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speaker boasts of spending a great deal of money, or says it regretfully.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية: إنه يقول إنه أنفق مالاً كثيراً، وهو يقول ذاك إما على جهة الافتخار أو على جهة التحسر

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf says he means the large sums spent on pre-Islamic acts called virtues, high deeds, and boasts.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) : "يريد كثرة ما أنفقه فيما كان أهل الجاهلية يسمونها، مكارمَ

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: One reading takes the utterance as proud ostentation against believers; another places it at Judgment, when the spending proves useless and is called destruction.
rows.anchor: جاء في (روح المعاني) : "أي: يقول ذلك وقت الاغترار فخراً ومُباهاةً وتَعظُّماً على المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling spending destruction suits the surah’s hardship and death: the Messenger’s companions suffered, the man imagines none can destroy him, the obstacle may be perilous, the hungry may die, and the left-hand group faces lasting ruin.
rows.anchor: وقد عبر عن الإنفاق بالإهلاك، فإنه لم يقل: (أنفقت مالاً)

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: Describing spending as destruction shows disregard: the spender treated his great wealth as wasted rather than expecting benefit.
rows.anchor: جاء في (روح المعاني) : "وعبر عن الإنفاق بالإهلاك إظهاراً لعدم الاكتراث

rows.speaker: التبيان
rows.claim: The spendthrift boasts of wasting wealth on desires; had he spent it where God commanded, it would have drawn him near God rather than destroyed it.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (التبيان) : "ثم أنكر سبحانه على الإنسان قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad is more exact than merely saying much because it conveys many things piled together; the Kashshaf notes its variant forms as plurals of lubda.
rows.anchor: واختيار (اللبد) في الآية مكان (الكثير) اختيارٌ دقيق ذلك أن اللبد معناه الكثير المجتمع

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf reports lubadan with damma or kasra as a plural of lubda or libda, meaning a mass and hence great quantity.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) : "لبداً قرىء بالضم والكسر جمع لُبدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The piled wealth echoes the disbelievers massing against the Messenger and Muslims to stop the call, paralleling their joint attempt to destroy his mission.
rows.anchor: فاجتماعُ المال في الإهلاك مناسب لاجتماع الكفرة على الرسول لإهلاكه، وإهلاك دعوته

rows.speaker: التبيان
rows.claim: Al-Tibyan notes that lam marks the past, matching the past-tense boast: does the person think nobody saw what he spent and destroyed?
rows.anchor: ثم وبخه بقوله: {أَيَحْسَبُ أَن لَّمْ يَرَهُ أَحَدٌ} وأتى ههنا بِلَمْ الدالة على المضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired verses invoke God’s power and knowledge, with seeing signifying knowledge; these are the basis of the warning.
rows.anchor: أنه ذكر من صفات الله تعالى القدرةَ والعلم الذي دلت عليه الرؤية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Continuing al-Tibyan’s proof, the author argues that God who taught people the two paths is even more deserving of knowledge.
rows.anchor: ومن جعله عالماً بنجدي الخير والشر - وهما طريقاهما - أليس هو أولى وأحق بالعلم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eyes given to the human directly answer his thought that nobody saw him.
rows.anchor: ارتباط قوله تعالى: {أَلَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُ عَيْنَيْنِ} بقوله: {أَيَحْسَبُ أَن لَّمْ يَرَهُ أَحَدٌ}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tongue and lips enable his boast that he spent a heap, so he uses God’s gifts while opposing God’s allies, messengers, and message.
rows.anchor: وارتباط قوله: {وَلِسَاناً وَشَفَتَيْنِ} بقوله: {يَقُولُ أَهْلَكْتُ مَالاً لُّبَداً}

rows.speaker: لسان العرب
rows.claim: Najd means high, firm, elevated ground, like a hard ridge rising before a traveler.
rows.anchor: جاء في (لسان العرب) : "النجد من الأرض قفافها وصلابها، وما غلظ منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two elevated paths are most commonly understood as good and evil; another view identifies them as the two breasts.
rows.anchor: والمقصود بالنجدين: طريقا الخير والشر. وقيل: الثديان. والأول أشهر وهو الذي ذهب إليه عامة المفسرين

rows.speaker: الرسول
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s explanation that the two paths are those of good and evil, and that one should not prefer the evil path.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة أنه عليه السلام قال: "إنما هما النجدان، نَجْدُ الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah uses najd rather than other Quranic terms for a path because climbing a height is difficult, matching human toil and the hard obstacle.
rows.anchor: ذلك أن التعبير مناسب لجو السورة فإن سُلوكَ النجدِ فيه مشقةٌ وصعوبة لما فيه من صعود وارتفاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ʿaqaba is a difficult, steep mountain route, named for the hardship of crossing it.
rows.anchor: العقبة: "طريق في الجبل وعر.. والعقبة الجبل الطويل يعرض للطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtiham means entering and crossing with force and hardship; quhma means danger, ruin, or a grave affair.
rows.anchor: والاقتحام: هو الدخول والمجاوزة بشدة ومشقة والقحمة هي الشدة والمهلكة

rows.speaker: البحر المحيط
rows.claim: Al-Bahr treats the obstacle as a metaphor for difficult righteous work, especially giving wealth like climbing a steep mountain.
rows.anchor: جاء في (البحر المحيط) : "العقبة استعارة لهذا العمل الشاق من حيث هو بذل مال

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: Al-Ruh says the obstacle metaphor stands for demanding, elevated deeds; making the named deeds an ascent after the two heights makes the metaphor especially eloquent.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (روح المعاني) : "وهي هنا استعارة لما فسرت به من الأعمال الشاقة المرتفعة القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He failed to repay God’s favors with righteous deeds such as freeing people and feeding orphans and the poor; approved giving benefits at God’s sight, unlike wasteful boasting, which is like ruined crops.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية أنه: "لم يشكر تلك الأيادي والنعم بالأعمال الصالحة

rows.speaker: التبيان في أقسام القرآن
rows.claim: The obstacle between a person and God is crossed by freeing a slave, feeding an orphan and poor person in famine, sincere faith and obedience, and mutual counsel to patience and mercy.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (التبيان في أقسام القرآن) : "ولم يقتحم العقبة التي بينه وبين ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma marks faith’s higher rank, not later timing: faith precedes deeds and is necessary for their acceptance; al-Kashshaf and Fath al-Qadir agree.
rows.anchor: جاء بثم لتراخي الإيمان وتباعده في الرتبة والفضيلة عن العتق والصدقة لا في الوقت

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf says mutual counsel means urging one another to persevere in faith, avoid sins, perform worship, endure trials, show compassion, and seek God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) : "المرحمة: الرحمة أي: أوصى بعضهم بعضاً بالصبر على الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience and mercy organize the surah: patience is needed for the Messenger’s abuse in Mecca and for raising children.
rows.anchor: إن السورة مبنية على هذين الأمرين: الصبر والمرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to mutual counsel in patience and compassion follows the discussion of the difficult righteous acts.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعد الآيات التواصي بالصبر والتواصي بالمرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is sealed over them without light, openings, or any eventual escape.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية: إنها عليهم "مُطبقةٌ فلا ضوءَ فيها، ولا فُرَج ولا خروج منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting عليهم suits the verse endings and restricts the sealed fire to disbelievers, since sinful believers may leave after punishment.
rows.anchor: فإن التقديم ههنا يفيد الحصر، فإن النار مؤصدة على الكافرين لا يخرجون منها أبداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza and non-hamza forms are both read; the author introduces why the hamza was chosen over the apparently simpler form.
rows.anchor: أما قراءة الهمز في (مؤصدة) فإنها قرئت أيضاً (موصدة) بغير الهمزة

rows.speaker: لسان العرب
rows.claim: The lexicon glosses hamzated muʾṣada as closed like awṣada and notes Abu Amr’s hamzated reading.
rows.anchor: جاء في (لسان العرب) : "أصد البابَ أطبقه كأوصده إذا أغلقه ومنه قرأ أبو عمرو

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: Al-Ruh says the hamzated form is a Qurayshi usage reported from Mujahid, while several of the seven read without hamza; both mean closed doors for intensified punishment.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (روح المعاني) : "مؤصدة مطبقة من آصدت الباب، إذا أغلقته وأطبقته، وهي لغة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavier hamza suits the day’s difficulty and the surah’s strain, and echoes the description of a heavy day in 76:27.
rows.anchor: فاختار الهمزة على الواو لثقلها وشدتها، لأن الموقف شديد وصعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humaza elaborates the sinner’s traits and punishment, so its extra image of columns fits that surah’s expanded treatment, unlike al-Balad.
rows.anchor: إنه توسع في سورة الهمزة في ذكر صفات المعذَّب وتوسع في ذكر العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humaza’s opening woe signals lasting ruin, so permanent closure and columns fittingly convey the permanence of punishment.
rows.anchor: إنه ذكر في أول الهمزة {ويْلٌ لِّكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُّمَزَةٍ} فدعا عليهم بالهلاك الدائم الذي لا ينقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hoarder who gathers and locks away wealth is repaid with sealed Hell doors and columns; al-Balad instead describes someone who squandered wealth.
rows.anchor: ذكر في سورة الهمزة أن هذا الكافر يجمع المال ويعدده، ويحفظه فكما حفظ المال وجمعه وأغلق عليه الأبواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the sinner imagines wealth will make him immortal in this life, he receives actual, everlasting confinement in Hell.
rows.anchor: ذكر في سورة الهمزة أن هذا الكافر يحسب أن ماله أخلده في الدنيا وأبقاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinner’s imagined worldly permanence contrasts with the certainty of his actual everlasting residence in Hell.
rows.anchor: فحسبانه الخلود في الدنيا مقابل لحقيقة الخلود في النار. فهناك ظَنٌّ وهنا يقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Humaza aggressor harms people and withholds all benefit, so he is imprisoned and the doors are secured; al-Balad mentions disbelief without those attacks.
rows.anchor: العمد الممدة على الأبواب لئلا تفتح. في حين لم يذكر في سورة البلد سوى الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Humaza offenders are disbelievers with added wrongdoing: they attack others, hoard wealth, and trust it to preserve them, meriting greater punishment.
rows.anchor: إن المعذبين في سورة الهمزة كفار وزيادة، فهم: 1- كافرون
